analysis.one_liner: Lets states opt out of ACA insurance rules and turn federal health subsidies into health savings accounts.
analysis.headline: Rick Scott's bill to let states replace ACA exchange rules with health savings accounts has sat untouched in the Senate Finance Committee since its November 2025 introduction, with only two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill creates a new kind of waiver: a state's governor or legislature could notify the federal government to drop most Affordable Care Act insurance-market rules, as long as the state keeps a program to cover high-risk patients. Federal subsidy money that would have gone to insurance premiums instead gets deposited into a new kind of health savings account the resident can use to buy coverage. States could also let private companies run their own plan-selling websites, and small employers in waiver states would get a bigger, simpler tax credit for offering insurance.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of states that opt in get their federal health subsidies as cash in a health savings account they can spend flexibly, rather than only as help paying premiums. Small employers get a 50% tax credit, no phase-out, no two-year limit, and can count up to 50 employees. Health insurers gain freedom to sell less comprehensive plans, and financial firms gain a new class of health savings accounts to administer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Waiver-state residents, small employers, insurers, HSA providers

how_it_helps.text: A state's governor or a majority of its legislature could notify the federal government to waive ACA exchange requirements and premium tax credit rules, provided the state maintains a program to mitigate risk to premiums, such as a high-risk pool.

Residents of waiver states would receive the subsidy money they would otherwise get as premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions deposited into 'Trump Health Freedom Accounts' — health savings accounts they can use to buy health plans.

The bill preserves the ACA's core consumer protections in waiver states, including guaranteed issue, no pre-existing condition denials, community rating, a ban on annual and lifetime dollar limits, rescission limits, and a medical loss ratio requirement.
Small employers in waiver states would get a 50% insurance tax credit with no income-based phase-out, a 50-employee threshold, no time limit, and seasonal workers counted as employees.

The bill requires federal regulators to update price transparency rules within 90 days to demand actual prices rather than estimates, standardized and comparable pricing data, and public reporting of provider outcomes.

analysis.who_pays: Residents who need comprehensive coverage could pay more or get less, because states may drop essential-health-benefit requirements and plans can be skinnier; the HSA money is capped at the national average silver-plan premium, so people in high-cost states may not get enough to cover a comparable plan. Account funds cannot pay for abortion or gender-transition care, which is defined to include vasectomy, hysterectomy, mastectomy, tubal ligation, and sterilization. Federal taxpayers continue funding the subsidies under a new name.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sicker enrollees and people needing restricted services

drawbacks.text: States can waive essential health benefit rules, so plans sold in waiver states may cover far less than plans sold today; the bill preserves sections of the Public Health Service Act on pre-existing conditions and rating but not the essential health benefits provision.

Subsidy deposits are calculated from the national average annual premium for a silver benchmark plan among non-waiver states, so a resident in a high-premium state could receive less money than their coverage actually costs.

Trump Health Freedom Accounts cannot be used to pay for abortion services or gender transition procedures, and the bill's definition of gender transition procedures sweeps in vasectomy, hysterectomy, mastectomy, tubal ligation, and sterilization, subject to narrow exceptions.

If healthier people shift to cheaper, less comprehensive plans while the ACA's community-rating and guaranteed-issue rules stay in place, premiums for those who remain in more comprehensive plans could rise — the same dynamic that made pre-ACA high-risk pools expensive.

The waiver condition that a state maintain 'an invisible high-risk insurance pool or another program designed to mitigate risk' is loosely defined, giving states wide room over how well sick residents are actually protected.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who want a cheaper plan and a flexible account, the bill offers real choice, and it strengthens the small-business credit and price transparency in ways that could help many people. But the bargain trades away comprehensiveness: skinnier plans and a fixed, nationally averaged subsidy deposit mean people with real medical needs — and anyone in an expensive insurance market — could end up underinsured, and the sweeping list of restricted services limits how the money can be spent. Whether this helps or hurts a given household depends heavily on their health and their state's choices, and the bill gives states few standards to hold them to.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on November 20, 2025, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Rick Scott of Florida introduced S. 3264, the More Affordable Care Act, on November 20, 2025; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
Two Republican senators have cosponsored the bill; no Democrat has.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — has been scheduled or recorded since the referral.

The bill's core would let a governor or state legislature waive ACA exchange requirements in exchange for redirecting subsidy dollars into health savings accounts, while preserving the ACA's pre-existing condition and rating protections.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has changed: current law still governs ACA coverage everywhere, so no group has gained or lost yet. The only party ahead so far is the status quo.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on November 20, 2025 and has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors are Republican senators — 2 of 55 in the caucus have signed on — and no Democrat has cosponsored; no vote has occurred, so the partisan shape is only beginning to show.

industries.note: In waiver states, insurers could sell plans free of essential-health-benefit requirements and could reach buyers through private commercial platforms in every waiver state, attracting healthier, lower-cost customers. The ACA's guaranteed-issue and pre-existing condition rules would still apply, but skinnier plans tend to shift costs toward people who need real care.

industries.industry: Health savings account administrators and banks
industries.note: The bill creates a new class of federally funded health savings accounts, with monthly, quarterly, or lump-sum deposits, creating new accounts for financial firms to administer.

Within 90 days of enactment, regulators would have to require disclosure of actual prices rather than estimates, standardize pricing so hospitals and plans are comparable, and publish provider outcomes data — more disclosure and compliance burden, aimed at making prices visible to patients.
Funds in the new accounts could not pay for abortion services or gender transition care, restricting which services the redirected federal money can purchase.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat untouched in the Senate Finance Committee since its referral, with only two cosponsors and no hearing scheduled. Most bills referred to Finance never reach a floor vote, and this one's realistic path forward would be as a provision attached to larger health or tax legislation; on its own, it is likely to expire at the end of the Congress.
